nameStory: The Rounded Snail gets its straightforward name from its distinctly circular, disc-like shell that looks almost perfectly round when viewed from above. Unlike many snails with tall, spiral towers, this little mollusk keeps things simple with its flattened, coin-shaped home that rolls easily through the leaf litter.
description: The Rounded Snail is a tiny terrestrial snail that you'll need to look closely to spot in New England's forests. Its shell is remarkably flat and circular, resembling a miniature brown disc or coin pressed into the leaf litter. At only about 2-4 millimeters across (smaller than a pencil eraser), this diminutive snail is one of our region's smallest land mollusks. The shell typically shows a warm brown color with subtle growth rings that spiral from the center outward.

idTips.label: Disc-shaped shell
idTips.description: The shell is remarkably flat and circular, like a tiny brown coin or button pressed nearly flat. When you pick it up, it feels thin and delicate between your fingers, with almost no height compared to its width.

idTips.label: Miniature size
idTips.description: Extremely small at just 2-4mm across - smaller than your pinky nail and about the size of a peppercorn. You'll need to get down close to the ground and search carefully to spot these tiny shells.

idTips.label: Brown coloration
idTips.description: Shell ranges from light amber to rich chocolate brown, often with a slightly translucent quality that lets light shine through the thin shell walls. Fresh shells may have a subtle shine.

idTips.label: Spiral growth rings
idTips.description: Look closely and you'll see fine concentric circles or growth rings spiraling outward from the shell's center, like ripples in a pond frozen in time. These feel smooth under a fingertip.

idTips.label: Paper-thin texture
idTips.description: The shell feels incredibly delicate and lightweight, almost like handling a fragment of thin paper or dried leaf. Handle gently as these shells can crack easily under pressure.

habitat: Look for Rounded Snails in rich, moist deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly under fallen logs, in deep leaf litter, and around rotting wood. They prefer areas with consistent moisture and rich organic matter, often found alongside other small forest invertebrates in the decomposing layer of maple, oak, and beech forests. You'll have the best luck searching in sheltered spots where the soil stays damp even during dry spells.

seasonality.spring: Active snails emerge as temperatures warm and moisture increases. Look for both live snails and fresh shells in the leaf litter as they begin feeding on decomposing organic matter.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when snails are most likely to be found crawling on damp mornings. During hot, dry periods they retreat deep into leaf litter and under logs.
seasonality.fall: Good time to find both active snails and empty shells as they prepare for winter dormancy. The falling leaves provide fresh habitat and food sources.
seasonality.winter: Snails are dormant but their durable shells can still be found in protected spots under snow cover and leaf litter, making this a good season for shell collecting.

funFact: Despite being smaller than a pencil eraser, the Rounded Snail can live for several years and carries up to 10,000 microscopic teeth on its tongue-like radula that it uses to scrape fungi and decaying plant matter - that's more teeth than a great white shark!
confusionNotes: The Rounded Snail's flat, disc-like shape makes it quite distinctive among New England's land snails, but empty shells might be mistaken for small seeds or plant debris. Remember the trick: seeds usually have a matte finish and feel denser, while snail shells have that characteristic smooth, slightly shiny surface and feel surprisingly light for their size.
contextualKnowledge: Many people walk right past these tiny snails without ever noticing them, but they're actually important decomposers in forest ecosystems. The name 'Gonyodiscus' comes from Greek words meaning 'angled disc,' referring to the shell's flat, circular shape with a subtle angular edge where the shell opening meets the body whorl.
compareHints: Since this is the only Gonyodiscus species in New England, compare it with other small disc snails in the family Discidae. The Rounded Snail is flatter and more perfectly circular than most similar species, lacking the slight dome or elevated spire that other small forest snails typically show. Its growth rings are also more clearly defined and concentric than in related species.
